Prompt engineering is the practice of designing instructions that guide a language model toward a desired response. In a RAG system, prompts can define how the model should use retrieved context and how it should respond when information is missing.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation, commonly called RAG, combines information retrieval with language generation. A RAG system first searches a collection of documents for information relevant to a user's question. The retrieved passages are then provided to a language model as context. The

provided to a language model as context. The language model uses this context to generate an answer. RAG is useful because language models may not contain the latest information or may generate unsupported answers. Retrieval allows the system to provide

unsupported answers. Retrieval allows the system to provide external information at the time of the query. A well-designed RAG system can also provide citations so users can verify where an answer came from. A typical RAG pipeline contains document ingestion,

from. A typical RAG pipeline contains document ingestion, text cleaning, chunking, embedding generation, retrieval, reranking, context construction, and answer generation. Evaluation is then used to measure whether the retrieval and generation stages are working correctly.

Reranking is a second-stage retrieval process used to improve the ordering of initially retrieved documents. A retrieval system may first return several candidate chunks using BM25, vector search, or hybrid retrieval. A reranker then examines the question and each candidate

reranker then examines the question and each candidate passage more closely. Cross-encoder models are commonly used for reranking. Unlike a bi-encoder that independently creates embeddings, a cross-encoder receives the question and candidate passage together and produces a relevance score. Reranking

A common architecture therefore retrieves a relatively small candidate set first and reranks only those candidates.

Vector search retrieves information by comparing numerical representations of a query and stored documents. The query is converted into an embedding, and the embedding is compared with the vectors representing document chunks. Cosine similarity is one common metric for vector

Cosine similarity is one common metric for vector search. It measures the angle between two vectors and produces a value indicating how similar their directions are. A higher cosine similarity generally means that the texts have more similar semantic meaning.
